query: What are the requirements for approving an aircraft or component for return to service under 14 CFR Part 43?
answer:
Direct answer
Under 14 CFR Part 43, the person approving or disapproving an aircraft, airframe, engine, propeller, appliance, or component part for return to service after an inspection must make a maintenance record entry containing: (1) the type of inspection and a brief description; (2) the date; (3) product hours, cycles, or life limits as applicable; (4) the signature, certificate number, and kind of certificate held by the approving person; and (5) an appropriate certifying statement that the product is approved or disapproved for return to service [S1][S5].

Who may approve return to service:
- The holder of a mechanic certificate or inspection authorization may approve as provided in Part 65 [S4].
- The holder of a repair station certificate may approve as provided in Part 145 [S9].
- A manufacturer may approve items it worked on under § 43.3(j), except that work must generally follow Administrator-approved technical data for anything other than minor alterations [S9].
- An air carrier operating certificate holder or an operating certificate holder may also approve (the excerpt cuts off before listing the full scope) [S9].

Watch out
None.

Where to look
- FAA 14 CFR Part 43, § 43.11 for record entry requirements and who may approve return to service: FAA_14_CFR_Part_43_Maintenance.html [S1]; FAA_14_CFR_Part_43_Maintenance.pdf [S2].
- FAA Advisory Circular AC 20-62E for detailed list of required entry items (type, description, date, hours/cycles/life limits, signature/cert number/kind, certifying statement): AC_20-62E_CH

query: How is a major repair or major alteration recorded and approved under FAA 14 CFR Part 43 Appendix B?
caution_trigger: Major repairs and major alterations require approved technical data (FAA Form 337, DER 8110-3, or STC) and cannot be returned to service on acceptable data alone.
answer:
Direct answer
Under FAA 14 CFR Part 43 Appendix B, a major repair or major alteration is recorded on a specific form (FAA Form 337) that states the item was repaired and inspected in accordance with current Federal Aviation Agency regulations and is approved for return to service [S1][S3]. Pertinent details of the repair must be kept on file at the repair station under an Order number [S1][S3]. The form includes fields for the date, signature of the authorized representative, repair station name, certificate number, and address [S1][S3]. For major repairs or alterations made by a person authorized in § 43.17, that person must perform the work and approve (certify) it to return the product to service, except an Aircraft Maintenance Engineer may not approve a major repair or major alteration [S1][S9]. Major repairs and major alterations for products not produced under an FAA approval are not required to be recorded in accordance with Appendix B of Part 43 [S2].

Watch out
None.

Where to look
- FAA Form 337 (Major Repair and Alteration) text and recording requirements: FAA_14_CFR_Part_43_Maintenance.html [S1]; FAA_14_CFR_Part_43_Maintenance.pdf [S3].
- Exception for products not produced under an FAA approval (no Appendix B recording required): FAA_14_CFR_Part_43_Maintenance.pdf [S2].
- Approval/certification authority and restriction on Aircraft Maintenance Engineers: FAA_14_CFR_Part_43_Maintenance.html [S4]; FAA_14_CFR_Part_43_Maintenance.pdf [S9].

query: What electrical load analysis requirements apply when performing an aircraft alteration under FAA AC 43.13-2C?
caution_trigger: Continuous electrical load must not exceed 80% of generator/alternator rated capacity to maintain emergency reserve.
answer:
Direct answer
Under FAA AC 43.13-2C, when adding equipment to an aircraft you must perform an electrical load analysis to preclude overloading the electric power system [S9]. The AC states that this analysis is required "when additional equipment is added" and refers to Section 3.9 "Electrical Load Analysis Procedure" [S9]. This requirement applies to alterations on nonpressurized areas of civil aircraft with a gross weight of 12,500 pounds or less, which is the scope of AC 43.13-2C [S1].

Watch out
The excerpts do not provide a specific caution block labeled "Cautions to check" for electrical load analysis; however, Section 3.9.1 explicitly states: "To preclude overloading the electric power system of the aircraft when additional equipment is added, perform an electrical load analysis…" [S9]. If you cannot locate a dedicated caution block in the supplied text, treat the statement in 3.9.1 as the operative guidance and verify against the full AC for any associated warnings.

Where to look
- FAA AC 43.13-2C, Section 3.8 "Electrical Requirements" (page 3-11) and Section 3.9 "Electrical Load Analysis Procedure" (page 3-13) [S11].
- FAA AC 43.13-2C, Section 3.9.1 "Available Power Supply" which defines the need for load analysis when adding equipment [S9].

query: Is chemical corrosion removal permitted on high-strength aircraft steel under FAA AC 43-4B?
caution_trigger: Chemical corrosion removal is strictly prohibited on steel heat-treated above 180,000 psi (180 ksi) due to hydrogen embrittlement danger; mechanical removal must be used.
answer:
Direct answer
Chemical corrosion removal is generally prohibited on high-strength steel without engineering authorization because such parts are subject to hydrogen embrittlement [S9]. AC 43-4B explicitly states that chemical surface treatment on high-strength steel parts requires securing engineering authorization [S1]. Additionally, acid-containing chemical paint strippers must not be used on high-strength steel due to the risk of hydrogen embrittlement [S3]. For highly-stressed steel parts (heat treated above Rockwell C40), corrosion removal is mandatory and must be performed carefully using acceptable methods like mild abrasive mats or cloths, but chemical removers are restricted without authorization [S5].

Watch out
The use of chemical corrosion removers is prohibited on high-strength steel parts without engineering authorization because these parts are subject to hydrogen embrittlement [S9]. Do not use acid-containing chemical paint strippers on high-strength steel as they cause hydrogen embrittlement [S3]. Overheating during removal can alter surface structure and lead to sudden failure in highly-stressed steel parts [S5].

Where to look
- FAA AC 43-4B, Section 6.72 ("Chemical Surface Treatment of Steel Surfaces") for the requirement to secure engineering authorization before using chemical treatments on high-strength steel parts [S1].
- FAA AC 43-4B, Section 6.13.2 regarding restrictions on acid-containing chemical paint strippers due to hydrogen embrittlement risks on high-strength steel [S3].
- FAA AC 43.13-1B, Section 6-165 ("Special Treatment of High-Strength Steel") for mandatory careful removal of corrosion and acceptable non-chemical methods like mild abrasive mats [S5].
- FAA-H-8083-30B AMT Handbook

query: What structural skin doubler practices apply to antenna or light additions on pressurized aircraft under AC 43.13-2C?
caution_trigger: Penetrating pressurized aircraft skin requires FAA-approved engineering data (DER Form 8110-3 or STC); AC 43.13-2C alone is not approved data for pressurized hulls.
answer:
Direct answer
Under FAA AC 43.13-2C, the following practices apply to antenna or light additions on pressurized aircraft:
- For light installations secured to a reinforced fuselage skin panel, the reinforcement doubler must be of equivalent thickness, material, and strength as the existing skin [S1].
- When replacing antennas, match the original mounting holes; any unused previous mounting holes must be repaired with appropriate hardware so the location is returned to its design strength [S2].
- It is highly recommended to use a structural backing plate at attachment points to strengthen the immediate point of attachment [S2].
- Before drilling holes in the aircraft skin, refer to the installation drawing to determine proper hole size and spacing [S2].

Watch out
None.

- FAA AC 43.13-2C, Section 5.8 (light/antenna installation doubler requirements) – location 59 [S1]

query: What mechanisms cause hot corrosion and sulfidation in gas turbine engine superalloys according to NASA research?
answer:
Direct answer
According to NASA research, hot corrosion in gas turbine superalloys is caused by liquid sulfate deposits (specifically Na2SO4) that act as a fluxing agent accelerating oxidation [S1][S5]. Sulfidation occurs through the interaction of sulfidation salt deposits with the superalloy surface, often under conditions involving cyclic thermal fatigue [S3]. The presence of salt contaminants from intake air, engine components, and combustion can melt at high temperatures (approaching 700 °C), forming a liquid salt mixture that drives these corrosion mechanisms [S2].

Watch out
None.

Where to look
*   **`NASA_Corrosion_Prevention_Gas_Turbines_19860012073.pdf`**, page 5: Describes hot corrosion as an ever-increasing form of oxidation caused by liquid sulfates [S5].
*   **`NASA_Hot_Corrosion_Pits_Fatigue_Disk_Superalloys_20090033745.pdf`**, page 13: Discusses the interaction of sulfidation salt deposits with cyclic thermal fatigue and pit morphology in nickel-base superalloys [S3].
*   **`NASA_Corrosion_Prevention_Gas_Turbines_19860012073.pdf`**: Contains an in-depth analysis of hot corrosion, molten salt attack (Na2SO4), and sulfidation mechanisms [S1].

answer:
Direct answer
The provided excerpts do not establish a specific quantitative effect of the cathode-to-anode area ratio on localized galvanic corrosion rates in aircraft structure; they only note that area ratios are a kinetic parameter influencing whether anodic corrosion occurs [S1]. One NASA study used a large cathode-to-anode ratio of 11 to 1 by selecting specimen dimensions, but it does not state how varying this ratio changes the corrosion rate [S2]. The excerpts do indicate that galvanic corrosion rates depend on differences in reaction activity between dissimilar metals and the potential difference between the cathodic and anodic members, with area ratios listed alongside other kinetic parameters as factors [S1][S7].

None.

query: What is the regulatory difference between a DER repair under FAA Form 8110-3 and an FAA-PMA part?
caution_trigger: A DER repair provides approved data (8110-3) for a specific maintenance operation on an existing serialized part; a PMA authorizes production of new replacement articles.
answer:
Direct answer
The excerpts do not establish a regulatory difference between a DER repair under FAA Form 8110-3 and an FAA-PMA part; they only describe the use of Form 8110-3 for recording DER findings of compliance with airworthiness regulations [S3]. The documents identify Form 8110-3 as a "Statement of Compliance with Federal Aviation Regulations" used by Designated Engineering Representatives (DERs) to record test reports, computations, and general analysis findings [S2], [S3]. One excerpt notes that a DER repair developed under FAA Form 8110-3 is described in commercial marketing material for repairing high-scrap rotable components [S1]. No excerpt defines an "FAA-PMA part" or explains how PMA status differs from a DER repair in terms of regulatory approval, form usage, or delegation scope. The closest relevant source regarding Form 8110-3 is FAA Order 8110.42D, which provides examples and procedures for using the form [S2], [S3].

Watch out
None.

Where to look
- For the definition and use of FAA Form 8110-3 as a Statement of Compliance with Federal Aviation Regulations recorded by a DER: FAA Order 8110.42D, Appendix I (location 34) [S2].
- For the scope of DER delegation to record findings on Form 8110-3 via test and computation: FAA Order 8110.42D, section 4-3 (location 19) [S3].
- For commercial description of DER repairs developed under FAA Form 8110-3 (not a regulation): Jet Parts Engineering technical marketing page (SOURCE-REGISTER.md entry) [S1].
